title: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service
desc: Combines theory, experiments and field evidence to show quality depends on incentives, liability and institutional design.

kps.k: Credence-goods economics frames expert-service quality as an incentive and accountability problem, not simply a shortage of consumer information.
kps.d: Customers may struggle to assess what work they need and whether the work supplied was necessary or adequate, even after purchase. The literature distinguishes undertreatment, unnecessarily elaborate treatment and billing for work not supplied; these require different safeguards. Fear of overcharging can also discourage future service use. Legal services appear as an application of this framework, but the supplied studies do not directly establish fraud rates or test remedies in legal practice or legal AI.

qs.q: The second problem mentioned earlier – putting a more expensive service on the bill than the one actually provided – is termed overcharging.

kps.k: Price incentives can eliminate fraud in theory, but only with specific supporting institutions and assumptions.
kps.d: Dulleck and Kerschbamer's baseline requires homogeneous customers, commitment after diagnosis and either liability for adequate treatment or verifiability of the service delivered. Under liability, uniform prices remove incentives for overtreatment and overcharging; under verifiability, equal mark-ups remove incentives for inappropriate treatment. Competition then affects who captures the surplus. These conditional results assume, among other things, observable costs and perfect diagnosis. Relaxing customer homogeneity, commitment or institutional protection can produce rationing, duplicated diagnosis costs or market breakdown rather than one inevitable outcome.

qs.q: DK06 show that the market will solve those problems by leading to equal mark-up prices: If the profit of the mechanic does not depend on whether he sells the new cooler or only a new gasket, then he has neither an incentive to sell a new gasket to a car owner who needs a new cooler nor an incentive to sell a new cooler to a car owner who needs only a new gasket.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

qs.q: We have shown that ineﬃcient rationing and ineﬃcient treatment of some consumer groups may arise if condition (i) fails to hold, that equilibria in- volving overcharging of customers or specialization of experts - both leading to a duplication of search and diagnosis costs - may result if condition (ii) is violated, and that the credence goods market may break down altogether if condition (iii) doesn’t hold.
qs.a: On Doctors, Mechanics, and Computer Specialists: The Economics of Credence Goods · Academia · 2006

kps.k: Controlled experimental evidence challenges the theoretical equivalence of liability and verifiability.
kps.d: Dulleck, Kerschbamer and Sutter vary liability, verifiability, reputation and competition across 16 conditions with 936 participants. Liability substantially improves efficiency, while verifiability has only a minor effect. Competition lowers prices and expands trade but does not improve efficiency without liability because undertreatment remains frequent. Reputation adds little when liability or verifiability holds. The authors favour liability clauses, but their experiment tests stylised institutional requirements, not the effectiveness or enforcement costs of particular real-world legal regimes.

qs.q: We study in a large experiment with 936 participants the determinants for efficiency in credence goods markets.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

qs.q: While theory predicts that either liability or verifiability yields efficiency, we find that liability has a crucial, but verifiability only a minor effect.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

kps.k: More information, disclosure and second opinions do not reliably improve outcomes; information design changes incentives.
kps.d: Balafoutas and Kerschbamer review models and laboratory evidence in which experts target high-risk consumers using information those consumers receive. They also report possible adverse effects from commission disclosure and ambiguous effects from second opinions; a dental field experiment reduced overtreatment only insignificantly, from 29% to 27%. Liu and Ma offer a distinct theoretical extension: with continuously varying losses, all equilibria in their model remain inefficient, even where customers infer losses precisely. Allowing experts to acquire an information structure enables a binary signal to achieve the first best. This is not a general claim that less information is better.

kps.k: Field evidence supports incentive-sensitive provision, while diagnostic uncertainty and social motives complicate simple profit-maximising accounts.
kps.d: The review reports inflated working-time charges in computer repairs and commission-driven financial recommendations; these findings remain setting-specific. It also reports a laboratory study in which diagnostic uncertainty increased fraudulent provision and reduced entry, lowering efficiency by about 16%. In Dulleck, Kerschbamer and Sutter's experiment, concern for appropriate treatment and restraint from exploitation explains some behaviour better than own-money maximisation, but leaves pricing and overtreatment patterns unresolved. The review contrasts evidence that promises reduce fraud with models in which honest experts increase customers' willingness to trust opportunists. Individual honesty therefore need not translate mechanically into better market-wide outcomes.

qs.q: The authors find robust evidence for fraud, mostly in the form of overcharging in the working time dimension, but also some evidence for overtreatment (replacing parts that did not need replacement).

kps.k: Practical safeguards should target the particular failure and account for the costs of changing service organisation.
kps.d: The literature distinguishes responsibility for solving a customer's problem from evidence that promised work occurred: accurate billing alone does not establish appropriate or successful service. Suggested safeguards include liability or warranties against inadequate provision, documentation of delivered work and separation of diagnosis from sales incentives. Separation looks more attractive when combining diagnosis and treatment offers little cost advantage and providers cannot collude. The experiment's preference for liability sits within the later review's broader, context-sensitive approach: neither low prices, reputation, disclosure nor professional goodwill supplies a universal remedy.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition that credence-service quality is governed by incentives, accountability and institutional design rather than consumer information alone, and materially develop it through complementary theory, controlled experimentation and research synthesis. Their common reasoning is that consumers often cannot determine either the appropriate service or what was actually delivered; accordingly, undertreatment, overtreatment and overcharging are distinct failures requiring different safeguards. Material internal variation concerns which institutions work and under what conditions. Dulleck and Kerschbamer’s baseline theory permits efficient outcomes through price design when customer homogeneity, commitment and either liability or verifiability hold. The controlled experiment qualifies that equivalence, finding liability much more effective than verifiability and showing that competition can increase trade and reduce prices without increasing efficiency. Balafoutas and Kerschbamer broaden the account further: disclosure, reputation and second opinions can be ineffective or counterproductive, so remedies should be context-sensitive. Liu and Ma add a distinct information-design result: precise inference can coexist with inefficiency, whereas a binary signal can achieve the first best under specified information-acquisition conditions. These findings do not establish fraud rates or remedy effectiveness in legal practice or legal AI; legal services are principally an application of the broader credence-goods framework.

qs.q: While theory predicts that either liability or verifiability yields efficiency, we find that liability has a crucial, but verifiability only a minor effect.

qs.q: Interestingly, in this equilibrium more information can be good or bad for a high-valuation consumer, depending on what the information reveals about the type of problem she has: Among high-valuation consumers, the most likely victims of cheating are those who receive a signal indicating that their problem is likely to be major, followed by the uninformed consumers and finally those who received a good signal.

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources accept the principal proposition that credence-service quality depends on incentives, liability and institutional design rather than consumer information alone, and materially establish its foundations. The theoretical source specifies the restrictive conditions under which verifiability or liability, commitment and customer homogeneity can induce honest provision, while showing that failures of those conditions can instead produce mistreatment, overcharging, duplicated diagnosis costs or market breakdown. The experimental source then tests key institutional mechanisms under controlled conditions and qualifies the theory: liability improves efficiency substantially, whereas verifiability has only a minor effect, and competition expands trade and lowers prices without ensuring efficiency when liability is absent. Material internal variation therefore lies not in whether institutions matter, but in the relative effectiveness of particular safeguards: the theory treats liability and verifiability as alternative routes to efficiency under specified assumptions, while the experiment finds liability markedly more effective. Both remain stylised foundations rather than direct evidence about legal practice or legal AI, and these curated sources should not be treated as representative of all pre-2015 scholarship.

qs.q: While theory predicts that either liability or verifiability yields efficiency, we find that liability has a crucial, but verifiability only a minor effect.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

elens.an: The 2020 review accepts the proposition’s core claim that expert-service quality is governed by incentives, accountability and institutional design rather than by information alone. It materially develops that claim by synthesising mechanisms through which additional information, conflict disclosure and second opinions may improve, redistribute or worsen fraud risks, and by showing that remedies such as liability, verifiability, pricing rules and separation of diagnosis from treatment work only under particular assumptions. Its internal variation is chiefly evidential and conditional: theory identifies possible equilibria and institutional mechanisms; laboratory and field studies provide setting-specific support or counterexamples; and social motivations sometimes reduce individual fraud while potentially worsening market-wide incentives. The review therefore supports context-sensitive safeguards rather than a universal intervention. It includes lawyers within the credence-goods framework, but does not directly test legal practice, legal AI or fraud rates in legal services.

qs.q: Interestingly, in this equilibrium more information can be good or bad for a high-valuation consumer, depending on what the information reveals about the type of problem she has: Among high-valuation consumers, the most likely victims of cheating are those who receive a signal indicating that their problem is likely to be major, followed by the uninformed consumers and finally those who received a good signal.

elens.an: In this curated 2023–2024 evidence, the source accepts the proposition that expert-service quality is not improved simply by giving consumers more information and materially develops it through a continuous-loss theoretical model. Both pooling and separating equilibria are inefficient, so even precise inference by consumers does not ensure efficient service. The source then identifies a conditional institutional remedy: when experts can acquire an information structure, a binary signal can achieve the first best. The main internal variation is therefore between an adverse equilibrium result under private expert information and an efficient outcome under deliberately structured information acquisition; this is not a general argument that less information is better. Legal services are presented only as an example of a credence good, so the analysis does not establish outcomes or remedies specifically for legal practice or generative AI.
